method: Same-agent English/Marathi close reading, recurrence-expansion comparison, reverse paraphrase and structural QA. No independent human or native-speaker review is claimed.
scope: The argument that primitive recursion and composition preserve computability, hence every primitive recursive function is computable.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: If h is defined by primitive recursion from computable f and g, compute the zero case with f and then successively compute h at 1, 2, 3, 4 and onward until the requested y-value.
samples.checks: The vector abbreviation, both recursion equations, every nested g-expression and the order of successive values are preserved exactly.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: A primitive-recursive definition produces a computable function from computable f and g; composition likewise produces a computable function from computable f and g_i.
samples.checks: The two closure arguments remain separate and both retain their hypotheses.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Zero, successor and projections are computable, and both composition and primitive recursion preserve computability; therefore every primitive recursive function is computable.
samples.checks: The conclusion uses exactly the base functions and closure operations from the preceding formal definition.

source_observations: T287 and MR-P129 directly support संगणनक्षम for computable while keeping it distinct from countable गणनीय.
T302 supplies the primitive-recursive class name; T288 and T053 distinguish primitive recursion from composition.
T042 and T253 support the successor and projection vocabulary used for the basic functions.
limitations: No independent human or native-speaker review has been performed.
The argument is informal computability reasoning rather than a machine-model implementation proof; the Marathi preserves that scope.
No TeX reader build was run for this source-only unit checkpoint.
